prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a complete and original achievement. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping thousands of atoms in a clean, light-shift-free environment, and Ye's group turned this into record systematic uncertainty and coherence, including the many-body, Fermi-degenerate clock and the comb-linked frequency transfer that makes comparisons possible. The result is a measurement capability that did not exist before: it underpins the roadmap for a redefinition of the second, tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, searches for new physics and centimetre-level relativistic geodesy. It is independently reproduced in many laboratories, the credit is a clean two-person pairing, and the interpretation is stable, so it is mature in the sense that matters for a prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterargument is that this is a refinement of a line already recognised in 2005 (frequency combs and precision spectroscopy) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems and ion clocks), and Bernhard's remark that it is more technological than conceptual has force. Credit is also not airtight: Lemonde, Hall's and Hansch's earlier work, and the NIST ion-clock groups all shaped the field, and the second redefinition has not yet happened, so some would say the main practical payoff is still to come. I regard these as real qualifications but not disqualifying, because the lattice-clock concept itself is new and the precision gain is several orders of magnitude.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are significant but more technological than conceptual, and overlap with the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes; he ranks B022 only seventh and puts the cavity method (B003) and magic-angle graphene (B028) first.
responses.response: I accept the overlap concern but disagree with the framing. The conceptual step was Katori's recognition that a state-insensitive 'magic' lattice can confine atoms without perturbing the clock transition, which is an idea about atomic structure and light shifts, not merely engineering. The comb prize gave the readout tool and the ion-trap prize a different platform; neither gave a way to interrogate many neutral atoms at once at 10^-18. I also note that B003 rests substantially on cavity-method foundations already honoured through Parisi, a stronger overlap problem than the one he raises against B022.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube (B002) first and B022 second, reading the clock as a transformative measurement technology with a clean two-person credit, while worrying that a single name for IceCube may misrepresent a collaboration-scale discovery.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of B022 and his attribution caution on B002, which I share: one name for a very large collaboration is a harder claim than Katori and Ye, whose roles are each well documented. I would not combine the two in a shared prize now, because that would be driven by overlapping support rather than a joint argument. If colleagues who know the neutrino field better can show that Halzen's conceptual role is decisive, B002 is a serious candidate in its own right, and I would revisit the pairing in round 2.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B022 first, arguing that progress is set by what can be measured, with Katori credited for the lattice concept and Ye's group for the record accuracy and many-body clock.
responses.response: I agree on the core case and on the attribution, but I would qualify his tolerance of B020 and B004 as near-equals. B020 has five credited names and uncredited theory, and B004 forces an exclusion of Schmiedmayer and leaves out Chu, so neither reaches the attribution clarity of B022. Where I differ is that I would not lean on the argument that the clock sets a new accuracy record as such; the stronger reason is the new physics access it provides.

responses.point: Danielsson puts the Higgs discovery through ATLAS and CMS (B037) first, as the experimental complement to the 2013 theory prize and a discovery of the first rank, while granting that any trio is a simplification of a collaboration of thousands.
responses.response: The scientific rank of the discovery is not in doubt and I put B037 third. My reservation is attribution: a prize to three founding spokespersons for conception and construction rewards institutional leadership, and the discovery itself was made by analysis teams whose leaders are a different group, as he concedes. That makes B037 harder to defend under the statutes than B022, and I do not think its being overdue substitutes for a precise credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes.
Whether the omission of Lemonde and others from the credited set is acceptable, and whether Ye's and Katori's roles are properly weighed against the NIST ion-clock work.

Whether a second prize part, for example IceCube, should be paired with this one, which depends on attribution arguments from colleagues in particle and astroparticle physics that I cannot judge independently.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, and training in Lindgren's group. None of these are credited candidates on the shortlist, and no specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from the provided profile, though B022 lies close to my own field of atomic structure and I flag that closeness for transparency.
